pillars.title: Quantum Tech
pillars.headline: Meet the machine behind the model.
pillars.summary: Qubits, control, connectivity, and noise determine which quantum operations a device can perform reliably. Learn how an abstract idea becomes a physical experiment.

topics.title: Qubits & platforms
topics.text: Superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, and photonics offer different ways to prepare, control, and measure quantum states. Platform comparisons require context about fidelity, connectivity, and the task.

topics.title: Control & compilation
topics.text: A hardware-aware compiler maps a circuit to native instructions and device connectivity. Routing can add operations, changing both execution cost and exposure to errors.

topics.title: Noise & measurement
topics.text: Environmental interactions and imperfect operations affect results. A simulator can model noise channels, but the model does not capture every detail of a physical processor.

workflow.title: Prepare
workflow.text: Initialize a quantum state. Preparation quality becomes part of the experiment’s error budget.

workflow.title: Control
workflow.text: Apply device-supported operations. Gate choices, qubit connectivity, and timing constrain the circuit.

workflow.title: Model noise
workflow.text: Explore how a noise channel changes the predicted state. Compare the model with measurements before trusting a hardware prediction.

workflow.title: Measure
workflow.text: Repeat state preparation and measurement to estimate a distribution. Finite shot counts introduce sampling uncertainty.

starter.title: Make noise visible
starter.text: Prepare |+⟩ in the qubit studio, measure in X, and increase the depolarizing mixture. Observe how the distribution moves toward 50/50. This is a teaching model, not a device benchmark.

pillars.perspective: A larger qubit count alone does not determine which useful problem a machine can solve.

pillars.title: Q Programming
pillars.headline: Write a circuit. Ask a better question.
pillars.summary: Use quantum software to express states, gates, measurements, and classical control. Start with local simulation, then understand the requirements of a hardware execution target.

topics.title: Circuits & measurement
topics.text: Qiskit and Cirq provide Python tools for constructing and simulating quantum circuits. Repeated measurements estimate observables or output probabilities; one shot does not reveal the full quantum state.

topics.title: Languages & hybrid workflows
topics.text: Microsoft’s Q# expresses quantum algorithms with classical control. NVIDIA’s CUDA-Q supports Python and C++ workflows connecting classical computing, simulation, and quantum targets.

topics.title: Targets & reproducibility
topics.text: Record the circuit, parameters, target, noise assumptions, shot count, and software version. GPU-accelerated quantum simulation is classical computation; hardware access has its own service requirements.

workflow.title: Define
workflow.text: Choose an initial state, a circuit, and a quantity to estimate. Make the experiment’s assumptions explicit.

workflow.title: Transform
workflow.text: Apply gates and compile for the chosen target. An ideal simulator and a real processor can produce different distributions.

workflow.title: Sample
workflow.text: Execute repeated shots or estimate an observable. Keep track of the statistical uncertainty and execution cost.

workflow.title: Compare
workflow.text: Check against a known small example or a classical calculation. Export parameters and results so the experiment can be reproduced.

starter.title: Build your first gate sequence
starter.text: Start in |0⟩, apply H, compare Z and X measurements, then try Z and undo. Export the run. Continue in an official SDK tutorial to implement a real program.

pillars.perspective: The browser lab builds intuition. External SDKs and cloud jobs run in their own environments.

pillars.title: Q ML
pillars.headline: Explore the learning loop.
pillars.summary: Quantum machine learning studies how quantum states, circuits, and measurements can contribute to learning tasks. Many approaches combine a parameterized circuit with a classical optimizer.

topics.title: Encode the data
topics.text: Basis, angle, and amplitude encodings have different qubit, normalization, and state-preparation costs. A large mathematical state space does not make classical data free to load.

topics.title: Kernels & trainable circuits
topics.text: Quantum kernels estimate similarities between encoded examples for a classical learning model. Variational classifiers instead adjust circuit parameters using measured outputs and a classical optimizer.

topics.title: Train & benchmark
topics.text: Compare against strong classical baselines using the same data splits. Include encoding, training, shots, noise, and inference cost. Some circuit families develop very small gradients called barren plateaus.

workflow.title: Encode
workflow.text: Map a training example to circuit operations or a quantum state. Count the cost of preparing each example.

workflow.title: Transform
workflow.text: Apply a parameterized circuit. Its architecture and initialization affect expressivity and trainability.

workflow.title: Read out
workflow.text: Estimate measured outputs and form a loss. Repeated sampling and noise affect the quality of that estimate.

workflow.title: Optimize ↺
workflow.text: A classical optimizer updates parameters and repeats the loop. Evaluate held-out data against classical models; a teaching demonstration is not evidence of a speedup.

starter.title: Understand the measurement layer
starter.text: Use the qubit studio to vary rotations and measurement bases, then study correlations in the entanglement lab. Follow the official lessons to train a small classifier outside this site; these labs do not perform ML training.

pillars.perspective: Broad practical quantum advantage for machine learning is not established. Results depend on the task, data access, resources, and comparison.

pillars.title: Advanced Quantum AI
pillars.headline: Connect ambition to the full resource cost.
pillars.summary: Investigate fault-tolerant learning algorithms and the classical AI that helps operate quantum machines. These are two distinct directions: quantum for AI, and AI for quantum.

topics.title: Quantum for AI
topics.text: Learning separations and proposed algorithmic gains depend on the task and data-access assumptions. Engineered examples, theory, and useful application advantage represent different kinds of evidence.

topics.title: AI for quantum
topics.text: Classical neural networks can interpret error-detection measurements or help analyze calibration data. AlphaQubit and NVIDIA Ising illustrate this direction; they are not general-purpose quantum neural networks.

topics.title: Fault-tolerant resources
topics.text: Plan for logical operations, physical qubits, error correction, runtime, and error budgets. Resource estimators compare explicit assumptions; an estimate does not demonstrate that the required machine exists.

workflow.title: Specify
workflow.text: Choose a precise learning or hardware-support task. State what is quantum, what is classical, and how data is accessed.

workflow.title: Estimate
workflow.text: Budget logical operations, error rates, physical qubits, and runtime under an explicit hardware and error-correction model.

workflow.title: Support
workflow.text: Study how classical AI can assist calibration or decoding. This supports quantum hardware rather than replacing an algorithm’s full resource analysis.

workflow.title: Validate
workflow.text: Separate theory, simulation, experiments, and program goals. Compare full costs and preserve the conditions of any claimed advantage.

starter.title: Start with noisy correlations
starter.text: Explore noise in the entanglement lab, then follow the decoder and resource-estimation sources. The lab models Bell-pair statistics; it does not reproduce a surface-code decoder or a fault-tolerant processor.

pillars.perspective: AI-assisted control, a logical-memory result, and useful fault-tolerant quantum AI are different milestones. Follow the evidence for each.
